event_description: State of Emergency - Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, Lincoln, and Pierce counties — between March 5 and March 24, 2014, a series of severe storms occurred in Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, Lincoln, and Pierce counties, producing extreme rainfall resulting in saturated soils, erosion, and issuance of flood and landslide warnings throughout Western Washington
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The region was under a transitioning weather regime through the first week of March.  March 1st came in dry and very cold under a modified Arctic air mass.  This kept soil temperatures below freezing across much of the northeast portion of Washington.  March 2nd into the 3rd brought heavy snow across these same areas as dry northerly flow was replaced by milder and wetter southerly flow.  This wetter and milder flow regime continued into March 5th, but with snow levels lifting above valleys floors.  A pair of Pacific storm systems bringing through more sub-tropical moisture into the region resulted in moderate to heavy rainfall in the valleys.  The first weather system during the early morning hours on March 5th resulted in a short duration mixed precipitation event for portions of the Northeast Mountains.  This lead to pockets of icy roads early in the morning before temperatures warmed up late in the morning and in the afternoon.  The main impact over this wet period was flooding over the Palouse, upper potions of the Columbia Basin and in the Spokane Area.  Flooding was exasperated by low elevation snow melt and frozen soils.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous county roads damaged and culverts washed out.  State Route 231 was closed from Reardan to the Stevens County line due to flooding over the roadway.  State Route 223 was closed from milepost 44 to 66 due to water and mud over the road.  A four foot section of a driveway was washed out due to a culvert being overrun by flood waters.  Flood waters inundated a culvert resulting in damage to portions of Hawk Creek Ranch Road.  Pooling of water was reported in Edwall due to culverts being overwhelmed by flood waters.  Damage costs for the event were estimated.

event_description: State of Emergency - Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, Lincoln, and Pierce counties — between March 5 and March 24, 2014, a series of severe storms occurred in Grays Harbor, King, Lewis, Lincoln, and Pierce counties, producing extreme rainfall resulting in saturated soils, erosion, and issuance of flood and landslide warnings throughout Western Washington
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level low pressure system in the Gulf of Alaska late on March 8th into March 9th directed a slow north to south sagging atmospheric river across the area. The origins of this atmospheric river were from off of the Islands of Hawaii. This resulted in abnormally high moisture content for early to mid-March. This was a very mild weather pattern with precipitation falling as rain even over the highest mountain peaks.  Moderate to heavy rain was reported in the Northeast Mountains, especially for areas closer to the Idaho border.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southbound lane of State Route 31 at milepost 11 was blocked by a combination of mud and large rocks.  Time of the debris flow was estimated.

event_description: State of Emergency (Eastern Washington) — GOVERNOR 14-04 WHEREAS, the month of July 2014 has been extremely dry, there are multiple ongoing wildfires throughout Eastern Washington, and current and projected weather conditions, in conjunction with existing and projected fire fuel conditions, present a continuing high risk of severe wildfires throughout all counties of Eastern Washington State
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The largest fire in Washington State history is now the 2014 Carlton Complex.  Central Washington was in drought status.  The fire was started by lightning on July 14.  The complex started as four fires; the Stokes Fire, The Gold Hikes Fire, the French Creek Fire, and the Cougar Flat Fire.  Explosive fire activity occurred on July 16th with very hot, dry, and unstable conditions in place.  Each fire then made runs over the ridgetops and grew into one fire between July 17th and July 18th as hot and windy conditions developed.  The fire rapidly spread through the communities of Methow, Pateros, Carlton, and Olema, and portions of Brewster consuming approximately 325 homes, barns, outbuildings and fences, utilities, cattle and livestock, and orchards, crops, forest, and range land in its path.  The fire burned 269,186 acres consisting of a combination of brush, timber and heavy fuels.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The lightning-caused fire, which began July 14, blackened 269,186 acres; leveled approximately 325 homes; 146 barns, outbuildings and fences; damaged utilities; killed cattle, wildlife and other stock; and destroyed or damaged orchards, crops, forest and range land. Total cost to fight the fire was approximately 87 million dollars.  The fire spanned two different public zones and cost and acreage is highly uncertain per zone.

event_description: State of Emergency (Eastern Washington) — GOVERNOR 14-04 WHEREAS, the month of July 2014 has been extremely dry, there are multiple ongoing wildfires throughout Eastern Washington, and current and projected weather conditions, in conjunction with existing and projected fire fuel conditions, present a continuing high risk of severe wildfires throughout all counties of Eastern Washington State
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Chiwaukum Complex was seven fires spread across Chelan County between Lake Chelan and the Highway 2 corridor.  The complex consisted of the Chiwaukum Creek, Shoofly, Mills Canyon, Kelly Mountain, Alpine Fire, Duncan, and Hansel Creek.  The fires were started on July 15th at approximately 0600 PST from lightning.  Hot and dry conditions on the 16th followed by hot and windy conditions on the 17th and 18th helped the fires spread rapidly.  Steep terrain in the East Slopes of the Cascades also contributed to wildfire growth.  The fire burned through a combination of timber including Ponderosa pine, grand fir, silver fir, mountain hemlock, sub-alpine fir, and slash.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Chiwaukum Complex erupted on July 15th at approximately 0600 PST and was started from a lightning strike on July 14th.  The complex of fires burned 50,540 acres. 543 homes were threatened over the 45 day period but none were lost. Four other structures were burned including one outbuilding and three seasonal cabins. The approximate cost for fighting the fire was 38 million dollars.  The Chiwaukum Creek Fire burned 13,895 acres; Alpine Fire burned 19 acres; Kelly Mountain Fire burned 124 acres; Shoofly Fire burned 163 acres; Mills Canyon Fire burned 22,571 acres; Hansel Creek Fire burned 1,073 acres; Duncan Fire burned 12,695 acres north of Entiat, WA.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed upper-level low was positioned over Eastern Washington on the afternoon of July 14th.  The cold pool associated with the low combined with surface temperatures in the nineties led to a unstable afternoon air mass and widely scattered thunderstorms.  Precipitable water values were near nine tenths of an inch, the afternoon sounding indicated an inverted V profile, and the presence of the upper-low led to a low shear environment.  Nonetheless, isolated storms became strong producing a combination of heavy rain, small hail, and gusty outflow winds.  Thunderstorm winds knocked down trees in two small areas of Spokane and Okanogan Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brush fire on Old Miner Road off Mount Spokane Road burned half an acre and two outbuildings.  The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

event_description: State of Emergency (Okanogan County mudslides) — on July 15, 2014, Proclamation 14-04 was issued proclaiming a state of emergency throughout Eastern Washington due to existing wildfires and the extreme risk of additional wildfires, including the 270,000 acre Carlton Complex wildfire in Okanogan County that continues to burn and has resulted in significant damage to homes, public facilities, and roadway infrastructure
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A downed power line was thought to be responsible for a twenty acre brush fire north of Deer Park near Eloika Lake.  It was not clear what caused the power line to go down.  Multiple outbuildings and vehicles were burned in the blaze.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 20 acre brush fire burned five outbuildings, a camper trailer, a horse trailer, an RV, and a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Saul Fire is believed to have been started from the same storm system that ignited the Buck Creek Fire (by lightning on July 22,2016), but the Saul Fire was not reported until almost a month later. The difference between how these two fires burned makes for a great example as to how fire spreads in environments that have, or have not, seen recent fire activity. It is believed that the Buck Creek Fire area had not experienced any recent fire activity over the last couple centuries, while the Saul Fire area had seen fire activity over the last couple of decades. The Saul Fire grew to 550 acres (as the most recent fire report of October 6th notes). This fire has yet to be reported as extinguished but is considered inactive (Having likely been controlled sometime during the late summer). The expectation is that winter snowfall will put it out.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated costs associated with mitigation/suppression of the Saul Fire was $7,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Deep North Fire, initially located 25 miles northeast of Colville, WA, was a human caused wildfire. The size of the fire was noted to be 596 acres at containment.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Costs associated with suppression/mitigation of the Deep North Fire were noted to be 5.8 million dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Cayuse Mountain fire , a human caused wildfire initially located 7 miles southwest of Wellpinit, WA, grew to 18,116 acres before it was noted as contained on September 7,2016. The fire stated when the Hart fire (which stated the same day on August 21,2016 near Davenport, WA) jumped across the Spokane River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated costs associated with mitigation/suppression of the Cayuse Mountain fire was 3.8 million dollars. It was noted that 27 homes were lost between the two fires (the Cayuse fire and the Hart fire).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Pickens North Fire, initially reported at 7 miles northeast of Tonasket, WA was a human caused wilfire. It grew to 760 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated costs associated with mitigation/suppression of the Pickens North Fire were $280,000.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Spokane Complex consisted of two fires. The Wellesley Fire located near the northeast edge of the Northwood neighborhood in North Spokane, WA and the Yale Road fire located south of Spokane and Interstate 90, and southwest of the small community of Valleyford, WA. Both fires started on the afternoon of Sunday, August 21, 2016 as a dry cold front moved through the area with strong gusty winds. As a result, both fires made very active wind driven runs during their initial runs on August 21.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Wellesley Fire was estimated to be 341 acres in size with two residences destroyed. |The Yale Road Fire was estimated to be 5,854 acres in size with  ten residences destroyed. Estimated costs associated with suppression/mitigation were 4.8 million dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The Hart fire, a human caused wildfire, initially located 13 miles north of Davenport, WA grew to 4,983 acres and was noted to be contained on August 24,2016. This fire jumped the Spokane river and started the Cayuse Mountain fire on the Spokane Indian Reservation.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated costs associated with mitigation/suppression of the Hart fire was 2.9 million dollars. The Hart fire destroyed 26 outbuildings and damaged 13 more. It was noted in news stories from the region that 27 homes were lost between the two fires (the Cayuse fire and the Hart fire).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic air mass invaded the region creating windy conditions over the Columbia Basin. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent winter storm brought significant snow accumulations to much of central and eastern Washington beginning on the evening of the 8th and peaking on the 9th of February. Along and in the lee of more exposed ridges in the Yakima and Kittitas Valleys and along the Horse Heaven hills blizzard conditions were observed with sustained winds between 35 and 40 mph (30 to 35 knots) and observed visibilities near zero.   Snow drifts in the Richland area as high as 5 feet were reported with some secondary roads remaining impassable for days. I-90 from Ellensburg to Vantage, I-82 from Yakima to Ellensburg and I-82 from south of the Tri-Cities to the Oregon border were all closed for significant portions of the day due to massive snow drifts and near zero visibility.  Across the region over 500 additional motor vehicle accidents were reported by the Washington State Patrol. In the Yakima Valley impassable roads and harsh conditions resulted in the loss of over 1700 head of cattle at an estimated value of 2.2 million dollars. Snowfall amounts ranged from 5 to 12 inches with 5 to 6 inches in the Tri-Cities, 5 to 7 inches in Yakima, 6 to 12 inches in Ellensburg and 5 to 10 inches in the Simcoe Highlands. Accurate snowfall measurements were very difficult due to blowing and drifting snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent winter storm brought significant snow accumulations to much of central and eastern Washington beginning on the evening of the 8th and peaking on the 9th of February. Along and in the lee of more exposed ridges in the Yakima and Kittitas Valleys and along the Horse Heaven hills blizzard conditions were observed with sustained winds between 35 and 40 mph (30 to 35 knots) and observed visibilities near zero.   Snow drifts in the Richland area as high as 5 feet were reported with some secondary roads remaining impassable for days. I-90 from Ellensburg to Vantage, I-82 from Yakima to Ellensburg and I-82 from south of the Tri-Cities to the Oregon border were all closed for significant portions of the day due to massive snow drifts and near zero visibility.  Across the region over 500 additional motor vehicle accidents were reported by the Washington State Patrol. In the Yakima Valley impassable roads and harsh conditions resulted in the loss of over 1700 head of cattle at an estimated value of 2.2 million dollars. Snowfall amounts ranged from 5 to 12 inches with 5 to 6 inches in the Tri-Cities, 5 to 7 inches in Yakima, 6 to 12 inches in Ellensburg and 5 to 10 inches in the Simcoe Highlands. Accurate snowfall measurements were very difficult due to blowing and drifting snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near zero visibility and sustained winds of 35 mph created treacherous conditions across the Yakima Valley. 1800 head of cattle valued at an estimated 2.5 million dollars perished in the storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Badger Lake, Williams Lake, and Chapman Lake, located 10 miles to the southwest of Cheney, were threatened by numerous wildfires started on August 16th. The three other fires were much smaller and contained shortly after crews arrived. While there were many structures threatened, no known homes or out buildings were lost.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Badger Lake Fire, 10 miles southwest of Cheney, started on August 18 by unknown causes and burned a total 244 acres of timber before contained on August 21. The cost of the firefighting resources required to contain the fire was calculated at 1.3 million dollars.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and persistent upper-level low-pressure system developed over the northern Rockies and southern Canada and then slowly migrated westward while continuously directing the jet stream and primary storm track at Washington State. This strong low-pressure system resulted in a 21-day period of a series of winter storms, wind storms, and atmospheric rivers that battered Washington State in rapid succession. First there was lowland snow the last week of December. Then a wind and rainstorm Jan 3 to 4. That was followed by two atmospheric river events from Jan 5 - 7 and Jan 11- 13 that resulted in heavy rain, minor to major flooding, and landslides. 2 flood fatalities occurred, and possibly a third from a landslide.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall of 6 to 10 inches, along with melting of remaining snow at lower elevations, lead to river flooding, significant urban and small stream flooding, and landslides. The peak of the rainfall was January 5 through January 7. Major flooding occurred on the Chehalis River and moderate flooding on the Satsop River. A motorist was stranded trying to cross a flooded road along the Chehalis River and was swept away when he left his vehicle. He was missing and presumed dead. Another man fatality occurred when an man tried to move his car out of flood danger and the car was swept away by flooding on the North River. Damages are reported and estimated; not all damages have been identified. Crop damages are unknown.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A prolonged period of northwest flow over the Pacific Northwest guided several rounds of moisture advection across the mountain zones, leading to upslope moderate to heavy snow showers nearly each day. Meanwhile, surface frontal systems and a series of shortwave troughs in the flow aloft produced moderate to heavy snow as well as some periods of freezing rain across the lower elevations. Strong winds were also produced as a result of these shortwave troughs and surface frontal systems at the beginning and end of the prolonged winter weather conditions. During this extended period of winter weather, the I-84 and several state and US highways in Oregon and Washington closed for extended periods of time due to increased traffic accidents from ice and/or moderate to heavy snow accumulations on roadways.

event_description: December Atmospheric River and Winter Weather Event, Emergency Assistance, and Truck Driver Hours Waiver
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An atmospheric river brought heavy rains to the Cascades December 8 through 10. The East slopes saw 48 hour rain amounts of up to 7 inches along the crest, 3 to 4 inches in the mid slopes, and at least half an inch in the low land areas. The rain combined with snow melt and led to several flooding and landslide incidents. The flooding forced the closure of highway US 2 for several weeks. An embedded cold front brought high winds in the 60 mph range to the region causing downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several reports of trees downed by wind in Chelan County. NWS Survey reported numerous snapped trees observed off of Mountain Home Road. Gusts of 77 to 82 mph on Tumwater Mountain weather sensor were recorded northwest of Leavenworth at 1600 LST. A trained spotter reported numerous trees down across powerlines. Blewett Pass was closed from 1800 Dec 10 to 1500 Dec 11 due to trees across US 97. Damage is estimated.

The rain combined with snow melt and led to several flooding and landslide incidents. The flooding forced the closure of highway US 2 for several weeks. An embedded cold front brought high winds in the 60 mph range to the region causing downed trees and power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station EW6379 Brewster located 3 miles Northwest of Monse recorded a gust of 60 mph at 0100 LST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow in the northern Blue mountains transitioned to rain the night of the 13th through the 14th, leading to rises in area rivers and streams. Portions of the Touchet river and Mill Creek eventually exceeded their banks, leading to flooding of residential areas and roadways across Columbia and Walla Walla Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Columbia County Emergency Managers office reported flooding of residences and water over roadways in the town of Dayton the morning of the 14th. Drone footage over Dayton taken on the 14th showed the Touchet river overflowing it's banks into numerous properties adjacent to the river, with flooding also along the Patit Creek that runs through the northern portion of Dayton.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Walla Walla County dispatch reported flooding along the Touchet River in the town of Waitsburg the morning of the 14th. The dispatch center relayed that a levee near the Preston Ave bridge had been breached, leading to flooding of properties along the Touchet River. Several roads in the Waitsburg area were also closed, including US Highway 12, due to water over the roadway.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precip amounts of 2 to 2.5 inches fell in the Palouse area from March 13 through the 14. It led to flooding in the City of Pullman.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: South Fork Palouse River flooding, with minor to moderate flooding in areas across Pullman, including downtown, Grand Avenue, and the area around the City Playfields. Water covered N Grand north of NW Windus St. NE Morton St by Reaney pool was flooded across all lanes. Grand Avenue closed from Nye to Ritchie. Main Street from Spring to Pine was closed. Morton Street near Reaney Park closed due to flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front passage and strong winds aloft mixing down to the surface the evening of the 11th through the morning of the 12th produced breezy to gusty conditions across portions of the Columbia Basin.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Juniper Dunes RAWS recorded a 70 mph gust at 0249 PDT on March 12th. The mesonet station PC048 located 14 miles southeast of Burbank recorded a 62 mph gust at 0330 PDT on March 12th. The mesonet station AV456 located 4 miles south southwest of Benton City recorded a 61 mph gust at 0210 PDT on March 12th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A high wind event occured over Eastern Washington overnight on March 11 to 12. A strong low level jet mixed down to the lower levels. It brought periods of high winds sustained in the 30 to 40 mph range and gusts up to 70 mph for portions of the region. It was followed by a cold front that brought snow amounts ranging from 2 to 8 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds with sustained in the upper 30 to 45 mph and gusts up to 58 mph. It downed a few trees and branches around the Milan area.
